findings.description: The repository still ships a set-based run-core CLI/projection alongside the new repository-wide session model.
findings.failureScenario: After migrating a repository to `docs/sessions/`, an operator uses the shipped run-core surfaces (`python -m ai_router.runcli ...` or the Explorer projection it writes). Those paths still require a set slug, discover work from `docs/session-sets/<slug>/spec.md`, and write `session-state.json` / `activity-log.json` / `change-log.md` back under `docs/session-sets/`, so the collapsed repository layout cannot be used through that CLI/projection at all. This is likely, not hypothetical, because the code remains live and its tests still seed and assert the old layout.

findings.description: Cancelled sessions are not actually skippable, and the next registration rewrites them back to `not-started`.
findings.failureScenario: A user uses the new `session cancel` flow to skip abandoned work, then starts the next session. `session.start` computes the next session from completed sessions only, so it still expects the cancelled session number; if the user re-registers later work anyway, `register_session_start()` rebuilds every non-complete, non-current session as `not-started`, erasing the cancelled state and its metadata. That is a likely main-path use of the new feature, because per-session cancel/restore was added precisely to cancel one session while leaving the surrounding work intact.

findings.description: Existing set-based run journals become unreadable instead of being migrated
findings.failureScenario: A repository that used the previous run-core version already has schema-version-1 `run.created` events containing `set_slug`, plus cancellation events containing `target` and `set_slug`. After upgrading, journal validation rejects those fields because the same schema version now has `additionalProperties: false` without them. Even if validation were bypassed, the fold has no mapping from legacy `(set_slug, session_number)` identities to repository-wide numbers. Existing run-core users necessarily have such events, making `status`, registration, and projection rebuilding fail on the normal upgrade path.

findings.description: The prior cancelled-session defect remains, with cancellation split across two independent authorities
findings.failureScenario: An operator cancels abandoned session N through the lifecycle session CLI and then starts the next session. The unchanged lifecycle next-session calculation still selects N from completed sessions only and registration can rewrite it to `not-started`. Meanwhile, the new run-core cancellation path records cancellation only as an `organization.cancelled` journal event and consults only `runproject.organization_states()`, so it neither consumes nor preserves lifecycle cancellation in `docs/sessions/sessions.json`. Cancellation of abandoned work is an advertised normal operation, so users who invoke it are likely to hit inconsistent registration behavior.

findings.description: Re-anchoring allows the author to omit part of the remediation from the next review
findings.failureScenario: After transferring a session whose dangling completion tree is unavailable, remediation spans several commits. The operator supplies the newest commit immediately before `HEAD` as `--commit`. That commit is a strict ancestor and is therefore accepted, even if it already contains remediation made after the previous review. `effective_baseline()` then causes the next verification round to diff only from that late commit, omitting earlier remediation. Selecting the newest ancestor is a likely recovery choice because the command provides no binding to the previous reviewed point.

findings.description: Version-1 run journals are still rejected rather than migrated
findings.failureScenario: A repository created by the immediately preceding run-core version contains schema-version-1 events. After upgrading, any command that reads that durable journal fails with `JournalCorrupt`; the only offered choices are to discard the active journal or keep using the obsolete router. This is probable for existing users upgrading the component and materially prevents continuity through the session-set collapse.

findings.description: Re-anchoring still permits omission of the first remediation commit
findings.failureScenario: After a round records an unreachable dangling tree, the author makes two remediation commits and supplies the first one as the anchor. `_legal_anchors()` accepts that first post-round commit, so the next review diffs from after that commit and never sees its fixes. This is probable because remediation normally begins immediately after the round, making its first commit the first commit after `recorded_at`; it can cause a reviewer to clear incomplete or incorrect remediation.

findings.description: The version-1 migration still strands valid repository journals containing multiple session sets or set-level lifecycle events.
findings.failureScenario: A repository-level journal accumulated runs from two session sets under the previous set-based machinery, then the repository upgrades to the collapsed session model. This is probable for any long-lived repository that completed more than one set—the old events carried `set_slug` specifically to distinguish those histories. `read_events()` now raises `JournalCorrupt` before exposing any events, so commands cannot read either the historical sets or the current set that the session plan requires migrating. A valid single-set journal is likewise stranded if it contains a valid set-level cancellation/restoration event.

findings.description: **Nit:** The re-anchor fix materially resolves the prior first-post-round-anchor defect for normally ordered timestamps. However, `_legal_anchor()` still equates Git’s second-resolution, user-controlled committer timestamp with actual commit chronology; a remediation commit with an equal or backdated timestamp can still become the selected “at or before” anchor. This is a low-probability clock-skew or timestamp-manipulation case rather than a typical-user blocker.

findings.description: Retired-set session lifecycle events still mutate repository sessions with the same number
findings.failureScenario: A migrated journal contains a cancellation for session 1 of an older set and a run for session 1 of the newest set. Because every set restarted numbering at 1, this collision is expected in multi-set repositories, and session cancellation is a normal lifecycle operation. Migration retains `session_number: 1` and adds `legacy_set`, but `build_projection()` sends all organization events through `organization_states(events)` without excluding legacy events. The older set’s cancellation can therefore make repository session 1 appear cancelled, despite its runs being correctly excluded from that session.

findings.description: **Nit:** The prior committer-timestamp re-anchor edge case is not fully resolved. `_legal_anchor()` still accepts the **first** remediation commit when that commit itself has an equal or backdated committer timestamp; the new test only backdates a later commit after two normally postdated remediation commits. This remains low-probability because it requires clock skew or timestamp manipulation.
